newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian tourism improving but long way to go.
newsitem.headline: Croatian tourism improving but long way to go.

text.p: Croatia has grand plans to transform its ageing coastal resorts into a world-class tourist destination but experts admit there is an uphill battle ahead to upgrade facilities and conquer Europeans' post-war fears.
As the 1997 tourist season gets underway, new research from the Tourism Ministry predicts that 24 percent more foreign holiday-makers will visit the country this year than last.
But the total number of tourists holidaying in Croatia will only be slightly more than half that recorded in 1990, before the former Yugoslav federation collapsed and war broke out.

In 1990 tourism is estimated to have contributed around 10 percent of Croatia's gross domestic product and was a vital economic prop. But the industry came to an abrupt standstill in 1991 when hotels had to open their doors to war refugees from Bosnia and Croatia and foreign tourists were scared away.
"Things are moving in Germany but it is hard to believe how some tour operators still fear for people's safety," Dragica Skare of Arcobaleno tourist agency based in Milan told Reuters on Monday.
Arcobaleno, which has offices in Frankfurt and Moscow, took part at this year's International tourism fair in Zagreb which gathered 230 exhibitors as well as 54 foreign tour operators.

To encourage their return to Croatia the Tourism Ministry launched a 14.8 million kuna ($2.5 million) media campaign in Austria, Italy, Germany and the Czech Republic and will give discounts to tour operators from 10 European countries worth 4.8 million kuna.

Croatia's long coastline with dozens of islands surrounded by clear water was seen as a trademark of former Yugoslavia. Ancient Dubrovnik, with its city walls dating back to the 15th century, was world famous.
Many resorts were only mildly damaged by fighting and the Yugoslav army took particular pains to spare Dubrovnik from extensive damage as it wanted to capture it whole.
Thus Croatia's main problem now is not winning the trust of foreigners but improving the poor quality of its facilities.

This month representatives of top hotel chain Hilton visited Dubrovnik and inspected some of its war-damaged hotels to see whether they could be upgraded to Hilton's demanding standards. Thomson holidays, part of Canada's Thomson Corp. are also said to be interested in the area.

Many hotels hark back to former Yugoslavia's socialist era -- large, concrete buildings designed for mass, low-cost holidays. Rooms decorated in orange and brown are a vivid reminder the hotels were built in the seventies.
Most are still in the hands of the state and so far progress on privatising state assests has been slow. Heavy taxes and a strong currency also combine to deter visitors.
Experts admit there is much to do if Croatia is to attract high-spending visitors rather than mass package tourists, possibly even demolishing old hotels and starting from scratch.
Recent research ordered by the government found the quality of facilities was not competitive while prices were similar to those in other Mediterranean countries.
"I cannot say that I am completely satisfied with the achievements so far," Tourism Minister Niko Bulic said in a magazine interview recently.
He said the ministry wanted to pressure the government into removing regulations which blocked competitiveness.

"Last year was the most successful since Croatia became independent. This confirms that we have passed the entrance exam for the tourist come-back to the European market...we have come to the international market to stay," he said. ($ = 6.019 Croatian Kuna)
